lines.text:
Life Among the Leaves — Exploring the Jungle

The jungle is one of the most biodiverse places on Earth. From the forest floor to the top of the canopy, every layer is full of life.

The canopy — the thick roof of leaves at the top — blocks most of the sunlight. Up here, toucans call to each other with their enormous colourful beaks, and parrots fly between the branches. Monkeys swing from vine to vine, and a sloth hangs upside down from a branch, moving so slowly that moss grows on its fur. An orangutan — found only in the jungles of Southeast Asia — builds a new nest in the trees every night.

Below the canopy is the understory — a darker, cooler layer where less light reaches. A chameleon sits on a branch, changing colour to match the leaves around it. A tree frog — bright green or red — clings to a leaf with sticky toes. Butterflies with wings the size of a hand float through the warm air. A dragonfly hovers above a stream. Spiders build webs between fern fronds.

On the forest floor, the ground is covered with fallen leaves, roots, and mud. An anaconda — one of the largest snakes in the world — coils around the trunk of a palm tree near the river. A tapir — a shy animal with a short trunk — walks through the clearing looking for fruit. Columns of ants march across the ground, carrying pieces of leaf many times their own size. Beetles, centipedes, scorpions, and termites live in the fallen wood. At night, fireflies glow in the darkness, and grasshoppers chirp from every direction.

The plants are as remarkable as the animals. Bamboo grows up to a metre per day. Orchids bloom on the sides of tree trunks. Ferns spread their broad leaves to catch whatever sunlight filters through. Lianas — thick, woody vines — climb from the forest floor to the canopy. The roots of some trees grow above the ground like buttresses, supporting trunks that rise forty metres high.

Water is everywhere. A waterfall crashes into a lagoon. A river winds through a ravine between steep cliffs. Streams feed into swamps where the water is still and warm. A cave behind the waterfall is home to bats and insects.

A jaguar — the jungle's top predator — rests on a rock near the river. Its spotted coat blends perfectly with the dappled light on the forest floor. An iguana suns itself on a cliff edge above. Caterpillars eat leaves, growing fatter each day before transforming into butterflies. Even mosquitoes have a role — as food for frogs, dragonflies, and bats.

The jungle is noisy, humid, and crowded. It is also fragile. When trees are cut down, the animals that depend on them lose their homes. Protecting the jungle means protecting millions of species — including many that scientists have not yet discovered.

lines.text: 'Who' is for people: 'The scientist who studied the frogs...' 'That' or 'which' is for animals and things: 'The monkey that swings from the vine...' 'The tree which grows near the river...' At B1+, choosing the correct relative pronoun is an important accuracy marker.

lines.text: ❌ "The jungle has a very unique ecosystem."
lines.name: ❌ "The jungle has a very unique ecosystem."

lines.text: 'Unique' means 'one of a kind' — it's already an absolute. You cannot be 'very unique' or 'quite unique,' just as you cannot be 'very dead' or 'very perfect.' 'The jungle has a unique ecosystem.' 'This is a truly remarkable habitat.' Use 'truly', 'absolutely', or 'quite' (meaning entirely) with absolute adjectives.

lines.text: 'Afraid of': 'afraid of snakes', 'afraid of heights', 'afraid of the dark.' Never 'afraid from.' Other adjective + preposition patterns: 'interested in', 'good at', 'responsible for', 'different from.' Each must be learned individually.

lines.text: 'A lot of' + plural noun takes a plural verb: 'A lot of animals live...' 'A lot of students study...' The verb agrees with the noun after 'of', not with 'a lot.' Similarly: 'A number of species are endangered' (plural verb).

lines.text: ❌ "The jaguar is the more dangerous predator in the jungle."

lines.text: ✅ "The jaguar is the most dangerous predator in the jungle."

lines.text: Superlatives: 'the most dangerous' (long adjectives) or 'the biggest' (short adjectives). Comparatives: 'more dangerous than' or 'bigger than.' 'More' is for comparing two; 'the most' is for choosing from three or more. Never 'the more' as a superlative.

lines.text: 'Jungle' is the everyday word, often suggesting dense, wild vegetation. 'Rainforest' is the scientific/geographical term. In formal writing, use 'tropical rainforest'. 'Jungle' can also be used metaphorically: 'concrete jungle' (a city), 'urban jungle'.

lines.text: Key terms for exams: 'endangered species' (at risk of extinction), 'habitat loss', 'carbon footprint', 'sustainability', 'ecosystem'. The IUCN Red List classifies species from 'Least Concern' to 'Critically Endangered'.
